blocks.text: 语音智能体能够处理日益复杂的对话，但有时导致通话失败的其实很简单：把一个名字、电话号码或电子邮件地址弄对。我们在 𝜏-Voice 中反复看到这一瓶颈：智能体弄错一个细节，还没能提供帮助就先在身份验证上失败了。

blocks.text: 𝜏-Entity 在十种实体类型（包括姓名、电话号码、地址和电子邮件）的 200 项任务上测试语音智能体。每通电话聚焦于单个字段，来电者配合，在被要求时会准确拼写。大多数通话耗时不到两分钟。

blocks.text: 基准内部

inlines.text: 基准内部

blocks.text: 每项任务都从一个缺失的值开始。智能体必须向来电者询问该值并正确提交。成功要求存储的值与预期值完全一致。我们改变三件事：值本身的难度、来电者的行为（如纠正和重新开始）以及音频环境。

blocks.text: 然后我们测量 Pass³：智能体能否在常规、高噪声和高语音条件下成功完成同一任务。

blocks.text: 知道何时放慢速度

inlines.text: 知道何时放慢速度

blocks.text: 当人们不确定自己是否听对时，他们会放慢速度、请对方重复、拼写名字或确认所听到的内容。智能体只识别出部分应当放慢速度的理由，而漏掉了其他理由。

blocks.text: 在论文中，我们还测试了规定一种验证策略能否弥合差距。规定的顺序是：询问，让来电者拼写该值或复述，确认并纠正，然后提交。

inlines.text: 在论文中，我们还测试了规定一种验证策略能否弥合差距。规定的顺序是：询问，让来电者拼写该值或复述，确认并纠正，然后提交。

blocks.text: 当智能体自行选择验证策略时，在所有三种条件下，只有 14–41% 的任务成功。规定的顺序将这一比例提升至 37–54%，根据配置不同，提升了14–31 个百分点。但额外的谨慎需要付出时间代价：每次调用会多花 21–28 秒。

blocks.text: 即使智能体意识到自己可能出错，也不保证能恢复。在论文的行为分析中，智能体验证的初始错误捕获中，最终只有 24–37% 被纠正。有时智能体会重复同样的错误。另一些时候，它会用一个新的错误值替换原来的值。只有当智能体能正确利用答案时，追问才有用。

blocks.text: 当一次调用需要多个字段时，错误也会累积。在论文的多字段研究中，尽管单个字段的准确率仍为 75%，但三字段调用的成功率只有 53%。在针对相同多字段任务的另一项对比中，验证每个字段并允许重试将成功率从 64% 提高到 82%。由于该干预措施结合了验证和重试，我们无法区分各自贡献了多少。

blocks.text: 方向是明确的：可靠的语音智能体需要识别不确定性、验证正确的内容，并在错误发生时真正修复错误。

blocks.text: 这些结果指向两个机会：更好地决定何时以及如何验证，以及在出错时进行更可靠的纠正。只有当智能体能利用答案来纠正其捕获的内容时，追问才有帮助。

inlines.text: 这些结果指向两个机会：更好地决定何时以及如何验证，以及在出错时进行更可靠的纠正。只有当智能体能利用答案来纠正其捕获的内容时，追问才有帮助。

blocks.text: 这并不意味着每次交互都需要尽可能长的验证过程。规定的验证提高了可靠性，但花费更多时间。挑战在于知道何时需要额外努力，并让这种努力发挥作用。

blocks.text: Voice agents can handle increasingly complex conversations, but sometimes the thing that breaks the call is simple: getting a name, phone number, or email address right. We saw this bottleneck repeatedly in 𝜏-Voice: an agent would get a detail wrong and fail authentication before it could help.

inlines.text: Voice agents can handle increasingly complex conversations, but sometimes the thing that breaks the call is simple: getting a name, phone number, or email address right. We saw this bottleneck repeatedly in
𝜏
-Voice: an agent would get a detail wrong and fail authentication before it could help.

blocks.text: Today we’re introducing 𝜏-Entity, a benchmark that measures whether an agent can capture a detail correctly, recognize when it might be wrong, and repair the mistake.

inlines.text: Today we’re introducing

, a benchmark that measures whether an agent can capture a detail correctly, recognize when it might be wrong, and repair the mistake.

blocks.text: 𝜏-Entity tests voice agents on 200 tasks across ten entity types, including names, phone numbers, addresses, and emails. Each call focuses on a single field, with a cooperative caller who spells accurately when asked. Most calls take less than two minutes.

blocks.text: Even in this simple setting, today’s voice agents struggle to get the details right.

blocks.text: Inside the benchmark

inlines.text: Inside the benchmark

blocks.text: Each task starts with a missing value. The agent has to ask the caller for it and submit it correctly. Success requires the stored value to exactly match the expected value. We vary three things: the difficulty of the value itself, caller behaviors such as corrections and restarts, and the audio environment.

inlines.text: Each task starts with a missing value. The agent has to ask the caller for it and submit it correctly. Success requires the stored value to exactly match the expected value. We vary three things: the difficulty of the value itself, caller behaviors such as corrections and restarts, and the audio environment.

blocks.text: We then measure Pass³: whether the agent completes the same task successfully under regular, noise-heavy, and speech-heavy conditions.

inlines.text: We then measure Pass³: whether the agent completes the same task successfully under regular, noise-heavy, and speech-heavy conditions.

blocks.text: This lets us separate two questions: Can the agent capture the value? And can it do so reliably as the conditions change?

blocks.text: How current agents score

inlines.text: How current agents score

blocks.text: On the 𝜏-Entity leaderboard, which pools all six 𝜏-i18n languages, GPT Live 1 leads: it captures the value correctly in 60.3% of regular calls, but succeeds under all three conditions on only 34.0% of tasks. Gemini 3.8 Live and Grok Voice Think Fast 2.0 reach 43.8% and 44.2% in regular conditions, and fall to 19.5% and 24.0% across all three.

blocks.text: Knowing when to slow down

inlines.text: Knowing when to slow down

blocks.text: When people aren’t sure they heard something correctly, they slow down, ask someone to repeat themselves, spell a name, or confirm what they heard. Agents recognize only some reasons to slow down, and miss others.

inlines.text: When people aren’t sure they heard something correctly, they slow down, ask someone to repeat themselves, spell a name, or confirm what they heard. Agents recognize only some reasons to slow down, and miss others.

blocks.text: In the 𝜏-Elicitation paper, we measured verification effort as the number of read-backs and spelling requests an agent makes during a call, then compared that behavior across familiar and unfamiliar entities, easy and hard values, noisy and clean environments, and different caller voices.

inlines.text: In the 𝜏-Elicitation paper, we measured verification effort as the number of read-backs and spelling requests an agent makes during a call, then compared that behavior across familiar and unfamiliar entities, easy and hard values, noisy and clean environments, and different caller voices.

blocks.text: Circles show the baseline; diamonds show the challenging condition. A move to the right means more verification. The caller-voice comparison uses each system’s own best- and worst-performing voices.

blocks.text: The agents in that study adapted to some kinds of difficulty: across systems, they verified hard and unfamiliar entities more carefully. But only Grok verified more under noise, and none spent more effort verifying the caller voice it struggled with most.

blocks.text: In other words, agents recognize some warning signs, but don’t reliably adapt to all of them.

blocks.text: Asking again is only part of the solution

inlines.text: Asking again is only part of the solution

blocks.text: In the paper, we also tested whether prescribing a verification strategy could close the gap. The prescribed sequence is: ask, have the caller spell the value or read it back, confirm and correct, then submit.

inlines.text: In the paper, we also tested whether prescribing a verification strategy could close the gap. The prescribed sequence is: ask, have the caller spell the value or read it back, confirm and correct, then submit.

blocks.text: When agents choose their own verification strategy, only 14–41% of tasks succeed across all three conditions. The prescribed sequence raises that to 37–54%, a gain of 14–31 percentage points depending on the configuration. But the extra care costs time: calls take 21–28 seconds longer.

blocks.text: Each configuration runs the same 200 tasks in each of three conditions under both prompts: 4,800 calls in total.

blocks.text: Even if an agent realizes it may be wrong, recovery is not guaranteed. In the paper’s behavioral analysis, only 24–37% of initially incorrect captures that agents verify are ultimately corrected. Sometimes the agent repeats the same mistake. Other times, it replaces the original value with a new incorrect one. Asking a follow-up question is only useful if the agent can incorporate the answer correctly.

inlines.text: Even if an agent realizes it may be wrong, recovery is not guaranteed. In the paper’s behavioral analysis, only 24–37% of initially incorrect captures that agents verify are ultimately corrected. Sometimes the agent repeats the same mistake. Other times, it replaces the original value with a new incorrect one. Asking a follow-up question is only useful if the agent can incorporate the answer correctly.

blocks.text: Errors also accumulate when a call needs several fields. In the paper’s multi-field study, only 53% of three-field calls succeed even though individual fields remain 75% accurate. In a separate comparison on those same multi-field tasks, validating each field and allowing retries increased success from 64% to 82%. Because the intervention combines validation and retry, we can’t isolate how much each contributes.

blocks.text: The direction is clear: reliable voice agents need to recognize uncertainty, verify the right things, and actually repair mistakes when they happen.

blocks.text: Where things stand

inlines.text: Where things stand

blocks.text: These results point to two opportunities: better decisions about when and how to verify, and more reliable correction when something goes wrong. Asking a follow-up question only helps if the agent can use the answer to correct what it captured.

inlines.text: These results point to two opportunities: better decisions about when and how to verify, and more reliable correction when something goes wrong. Asking a follow-up question only helps if the agent can use the answer to correct what it captured.

blocks.text: That doesn’t mean every interaction needs the longest possible verification process. Prescribed verification improves reliability, but takes more time. The challenge is knowing when that extra effort is needed and making it count.
